summary:
The Democratic Republic of Congo does not criminalise same-sex conduct. Same-sex activity has never been outlawed, including under Belgian colonial rule, and the age of consent is equal for all partners. A stakeholder submission to the country's 5th-cycle Universal Periodic Review (Savie asbl and co-signatories, March 2024) states that the state neither protects nor promotes LGBTIQ+ rights, so the absence of a ban carries no accompanying legal safeguard.

Public same-sex affection can be prosecuted under Article 176 of the Penal Code, which punishes anyone who publicly outrages morals by actions, and local ordinances are also applied against LGBTQ people. Queer In The World reports that LGBT expression is censored and can expose a person to imprisonment. Because the exposure arises from police and administrative discretion rather than a dedicated offence, a visitor's conduct is judged case by case by the officer in front of them.

Trans visitors have no route to legal gender recognition: the country offers no gender-identity recognition and no legal gender change. Documents will be read exactly as issued at hotels, banks, checkpoints and border posts, with no domestic mechanism to align them with a person's lived gender.

Violence, harassment and torture against LGBT people are reported as involving the police, the security forces and the army. Queer In The World advises visitors to keep a low profile and exercise discretion, and the GayOut travel guide rates the country high risk for LGBTQ travellers.

Armed militia groups in eastern DR Congo have committed extreme violence against LGBTQ people with near-total impunity, and the collapse of state authority in contested areas means that formal legal protections are theoretical there.

There is no relationship recognition of any kind and same-sex marriage has been banned constitutionally since 2006. Church groups actively promote the view that homosexuality is immoral, which shapes the social environment a visitor enters alongside the legal one.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch reported on 4 December 2017, drawing on more than 120 interviews including nine Congolese security-force officers, UN officials and 21 M23 fighters, that security forces recruited ex-M23 fighters from Uganda and Rwanda between October and December 2016 and deployed them with orders to use lethal force against protesters in Kinshasa, Goma and Lubumbashi. The documented pattern of state violence and impunity bears directly on how a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor can expect any complaint or protection request to be handled.

The country's formal legal position places it among jurisdictions with no sodomy statute but also no protective framework, so risk is set by enforcement practice rather than by a written penalty. Where central authority thins out, as in the east, that enforcement practice is replaced by armed-group violence, which is the sharpest divergence a visitor will encounter between regions of the same country.
localsOnly:
Residents live under a legal regime that neither bans nor protects: Article 176 of the Penal Code reaches public conduct judged to outrage morals, and municipal ordinances are used against LGBTQ people, while no anti-discrimination, hate-crime or recognition provisions exist to offset that exposure.

There is no legal gender recognition and no procedure for changing gender markers on official documents, so trans Congolese carry identity papers that do not reflect their gender for the duration of their lives.

Same-sex partners have no standing: marriage is constitutionally barred to them since 2006 and no other form of relationship recognition exists, which affects inheritance, hospital visitation, next-of-kin designation and custody.

The stakeholder submission to the 5th-cycle Universal Periodic Review records the community's formal position that the state neither protects nor promotes LGBTIQ+ rights, and church messaging framing homosexuality as immoral shapes employment, housing and family exposure.

Reports of violence, harassment and torture by police, security forces and army personnel mean that reporting a crime carries a credible risk of further victimisation rather than remedy.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory supplies a fragment of Article 176 of the Penal Code but not the full current text of the provision, and the specific local ordinances invoked against LGBTQ people are not enumerated or dated.

Unresolved: no source here documents how often Article 176 or the indecency provisions are actually charged and with what outcomes, so enforcement frequency rests on general reporting rather than case data.

Not sourced in this inventory: entry and visa screening, airport or border document checks, and whether gender-nonconforming presentation draws secondary inspection on arrival. Nothing here should be read as describing border procedure.

Not sourced: access to gender-affirming medical care, HIV prevention or treatment for visitors, and whether these are restricted in law.

Unresolved: the Human Rights Watch findings cover recruitment and deployments between October and December 2016 reported in December 2017; the current posture of the security forces toward protest and assembly is not established by these sources.

Provenance caveat: the relationship-recognition, marriage and age-of-consent claims come from Wikiwand, a mirror of Wikipedia, so they inherit Wikipedia's underlying sourcing rather than independent verification; the Queer In The World page was last updated 3 December 2023 and covers both Congos, and only its DR Congo-specific content is reflected here.
